utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Good afternoon and welcome to today's New York City Council hearing on Committee on Sanitation and Solid Waste Management.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: During this time, during today's hearing, no one may approach the dais.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff

chapters.summary: Chair Justin Sanchez opens the hearing, thanks attendees for caring about waste equity, and introduces himself as committee chair. He notes the late start time, welcomes committee members and administration representatives, and confirms no one is on Zoom initially.
chapters.title: Chair Sanchez calls meeting to order and welcomes attendees

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you, Roman.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Oh, good afternoon, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: I think this is the latest start time that we've ever had to this committee.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone, and welcome to today's committee on sanitation and solid waste management.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: I want to give all of you guys that are actually in here a round of applause.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you for joining us.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you for caring about waste equity in our city.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Having said that...

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: My name is Justin Sanchez.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: I am a council member and proud chair of this committee.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: I want to thank all members of the committee and the representatives of the admin for joining us today.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: The council members who are here present with us are Council Member Zhuang, Council Member Lewis, Council Member Hankerson,

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: I see no one on Zoom.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you, everyone, for your wide attendance.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Today's purpose of today's oversight hearing is to learn more about the city's implementation of the waste equity law.

chapters.summary: Sanchez explains that the oversight hearing examines implementation of Local Law 152 of 2018, the waste equity law. He describes how environmental justice communities face disproportionate truck traffic, noise, air pollution, and health harms including asthma and low birth weights.
chapters.title: Sanchez explains Waste Equity Law purpose and health impacts

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: So this was passed as Local Law 152 in 2018, and to assess our progress on reducing the negative impacts of the city's waste collection, recycling, and transfer industry on vulnerable New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: New York City's most economically disadvantaged communities and communities of color.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Hi, my district.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Tend to face disproportionate health hazards associated with waste transfer infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Specifically, Bronx 1 and 2, hi.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Exposure to heavy truck traffic and the accompanying noise, air pollution, and odor have been linked to various negative health and developmental outcomes, including, but not limited to, reduced intellectual,

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: development in children, increased incidence of asthma, and heightened risk of heart defects and low birth weights in babies when birthing parents are exposed to truck emissions during pregnancy.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: I'd also like to note that we've been welcomed by Councilmember Wilson.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Oh, and a truck sounded just in that time.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: If you could hear that.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: The waste equity laws mandated reduction in private transfer station capacity.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: are meant to help to alleviate some of these harms experienced by environmental justice communities, also commonly referred to during this hearing as EJ communities, and to encourage means of transferring waste that avoid diesel trucks.

chapters.summary: Sanchez identifies Brooklyn Community District 1, Queens Community District 12, and Bronx Community Districts 1 and 2 as the four designated districts required to reduce waste transfer capacity. He explains the law's reporting and notification requirements on DSNY.
chapters.title: Sanchez outlines designated districts and reporting requirements

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Every waste transfer station located in four of the city's most burdened community districts.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: That includes Brooklyn Community District 1, Queens Community District 12, and Bronx Community Districts 1 and Community District 2.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: None in Manhattan.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Were required to comply with waste capacity reductions.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: In order to ensure effective oversight, the Waste Equity Law imposed reporting and notification requirements on the Department of Sanitation to track the permitted capacity in different waste transportations,

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: track any impacts on employment from these reductions, alert the mayor and the council in the event that a waste transportation approaches or exceeds their total permitted capacity,

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: and report on the feasibility of reducing truck traffic in residential neighborhoods through means other than capacity reductions.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Since 2019, DSNY has complied with the law's reporting requirements by publishing annual implementation reports and providing the relevant data for that year.

chapters.summary: Sanchez cites the 2025 Waste Equity Law Implementation Annual Report showing a 15% citywide decrease in waste transfer volume. However, he notes that none of the four designated districts have achieved full compliance with required capacity reductions.
chapters.title: Sanchez reports 15% citywide waste decrease but no full compliance

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: The most recent Waste Equity Law Implementation Annual Report for calendar year 2025 was just released last month.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: We are pleased that DSNY's data shows that overall,

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: The waste transportation volume is approximately 6.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: 15,083 tons per day, which represents a 15% decrease in the waste transfer volume citywide.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: I want to underscore that, citywide in the law's passage.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: However, that being said, we are concerned that none, zero,

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: of the four designated community districts slated for the mandated reductions in permitted private transfer station capacity have achieved full compliance with the reduction of the requirements of the waste equity law.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Additionally, we are worried that the permitted capacity reductions we have seen

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: targeted mostly unused capacity at waste transfer stations, and that two stations appear to have not gone any reduction whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And just so that everyone is on the same page.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: So out of the four community districts that we spoke about, Brooklyn CD1, Queen CD12, Bronx CD1, and Bronx CD2.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Brooklyn CD1 was supposed to have a 50% reduction in capacity, whereas Queens CD12, Bronx 1, and Bronx 2 were supposed to have a 33% reduction in capacity, and none of those targets have been hit.

chapters.summary: Sanchez acknowledges progress but says the city remains far from equitable distribution of waste transfer infrastructure. He states that approximately 74% of citywide throughput remains concentrated in the four designated community districts.
chapters.title: Sanchez notes 74% of waste remains concentrated in four districts

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: So having said that, despite progress on the waste equity laws, we want to be clear that we have seen a 15% reduction in the city wide.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: So there has been progress.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Despite that progress, the city is far from achieving its equitable distribution of the burdens of waste.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: transfer infrastructure citywide.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: To date, approximately 74% of citywide throughput, the average daily amount of solid waste delivered from a solid waste transfer station,

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: remains concentrated in the four designated community districts.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: We look forward to hearing from DSNY and advocates about the implementation challenges and the shortcomings of the waste equity law and the city's plans to fulfill the law's requirements as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: We also look forward to discussing proposals to improve waste infrastructure

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: inequities borne by these communities.

chapters.summary: Sanchez previews five bills: Intro 30 on city-owned building containerization, Intro 987 on association-requested containers, Intro 352 on rechargeable battery disposal, Intro 401 on public organic waste receptacles, and Intro 1041 on litter basket removals.
chapters.title: Sanchez previews five bills on containerization, batteries, organics, litter baskets

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: In addition to the oversight, we will be hearing five bills today.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: First, intro number 30.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Oh, before I start that, we've been welcomed by Councilmember Epstein.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: First, intro number 30, sponsored by Majority Leader Abreu and Councilmember Lewis,

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: would require the city to create a program that would mandate city-owned non-residential buildings to dispose of their waste in stationary on-street containers.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Intro number 987, also sponsored by Majority Leader Abreu and Councilmember Ressler, would allow block associations and nonprofit associations to request stationary on-street waste containers for the storage and collection of waste.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Next up, intro number 352, sponsored by Councilmember Nurse.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Which would require DSNY to develop a plan for ensuring proper disposal of rechargeable batteries

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: used for powered mobility devices, such as motorized bicycles and scooters.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: We are also hearing Intro 401, sponsored by Councilmember Ressler, which would require DSNY to install a minimum number of public organic waste receptacles in every community district.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Finally, Intro number 1041, sponsored by Councilmember Hankerson.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: This bill would bar DSNY from removing public litter baskets solely on the basis that they were used for illegal dumping,

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: requiring notification to council members and community boards when a removal is proposed, and publishing data around why baskets were removed and why.

chapters.summary: Chair Sanchez passes the floor and microphone to Council Member Ty Hankerson to discuss his bill.
chapters.title: Sanchez yields floor to Council Member Hankerson

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: I now pass the floor and the mic to Councilmember Hankerson to discuss his bill.

chapters.summary: Council Member Hankerson argues that DSNY's past practice of removing litter baskets due to illegal dumping punished entire neighborhoods. He explains that Intro 1041 would bar removals solely for illegal dumping, require notification to council members and community boards, and mandate reporting on removals.
chapters.title: Hankerson introduces Intro 1041 on litter basket removals

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: For years, New Yorkers have been calling for cleaner streets and better sanitation services to improve the quality of life in their neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Residents have continuously pushed for more public litter baskets, and council members have even allocated funding to DSNY to bring more baskets into their districts.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Yet, despite these efforts, there never seemed to be enough.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Part of the reason is a shameful practice by DSNY, at least I think it's shameful, of routinely removing public litter baskets in response to illegal dumping or the disposal of household garbage, which the department categorizes as improper use of these baskets.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: In doing so,

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Entire neighborhoods of thousands of residents are being punished for the actions of the

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: few bad actors.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: And instead of addressing the people responsible for the dumping, we are taking away a service that the rest of the community is in so desperate need of.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: In Southeast Queens, where I represent, we have spent a great deal of time fighting to get our streets clean and to keep them clean.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: I understand the frustration that comes with repeatedly cleaning the same location, only to return the next morning and find it covered in improper waste again.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: But removing a litter basket does very little to address the behavior.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Now, the DSNY has stated that it no longer engages in this practice, and I welcome that change.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: But I believe it is in our best interest, Mr.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Chair, for our communities to codify that protection into law so that it remains the standard regardless of who is leading the agency or the city.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Under Intro 1041, DSNY would no longer be permitted to remove a public litter basket solely on the grounds of illegal dumping.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: The bill would require the department to notify the local council member and community board before removing the basket and give them 10 business days to respond.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Our local community boards and elected officials hear directly from residents about the situation, I'm sorry, about the sanitation conditions in their neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: They should have an opportunity to weigh in before a service is taken away from the very people that they represent.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: The legislation will require reporting on basket removals and subsequent litter complaints, giving us a better understanding of whether these decisions are

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: are actually improving the conditions of the neighborhoods that we represent and live in day after day.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: New Yorkers pay taxes for sanitation services, and they have every right to expect those services to be maintained.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: If someone is abusing a litter basket, then our attention should be directed to the person responsible.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: We should be increasing enforcement against illegal dumping and working with communities to address these problem locations, rather than reducing the very services residents have fought to receive.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: I am proud to sponsor this legislation and look forward to working with my colleagues to get it passed.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Chair.

chapters.title: Sanchez thanks Hankerson, staff, and outlines testimony order

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Councilmember Hankerson.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: I look forward to the dialogue regarding these bills today.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: I would also like to thank everyone and my team, especially my legislative director, River Alexander, for all of the work in getting this together, and the Sanitation Committee staff, especially Samia Schell.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And last time we shouted out Samia, but this time I really want to make sure that we're shouting out Natasha Bynum, who is also our co-counsel on this committee, and we are so excited by the work.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And I want to make sure before we continue that we have also been joined by the amazing Councilmember Hanif via Zoom.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember Hanif.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And with that, I want to make sure I'm not forgetting anything.

utterances.text: We will start by hearing testimony from the Department of Sanitation, followed by some questions to the agency, and then we will hear testimony from the public.

chapters.summary: Commissioner Gregory Anderson introduces himself and Deputy Commissioner Jen McDonald. He says DSNY provides free, unlimited sanitation service to all New Yorkers and acknowledges that the waste system reflects longstanding injustices.
chapters.title: Commissioner Anderson introduces DSNY equity mission

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Sanchez and members of the City Council Committee on Sanitation and Solid Waste Management.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: I'm Gregory Anderson, Commissioner of the New York City Department of Sanitation, and I am joined by Jen McDonald, our Deputy Commissioner for Solid Waste Management.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: The Department of Sanitation has equity baked into our functions at the deepest structural level, in that we provide

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: a free, unlimited service to all New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: There's no sign up, there's no opt in, there's no fee for collection or limit on how much you can set out.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Just put your waste at the curb, properly sorted, and in a container, and we'll come get it.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And sanitation serves everyone without question and is committed to fairness.

chapters.summary: Anderson describes the 2006 Solid Waste Management Plan's shift from truck export to rail and barge export. He explains that Local Law 152 required capacity reductions in four overburdened districts and allowed exemptions for recycling, organics, and rail-export facilities.
chapters.title: Anderson details 2006 solid waste plan and Local Law 152

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: We also acknowledge that our waste management and export system reflects longstanding injustices and inequities.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: To begin to correct these, we have implemented the city's landmark 2006 solid waste management plan, which called for a move away from truck export of solid waste from New York City to more sustainable and equitable rail and barge export.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: The facilities and system built as a result of that plan represent billions of dollars in investment, both public and private, in equitable, sustainable waste management systems and have reduced truck traffic.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: in historically overburdened communities by hundreds of trips per day.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: We did not stop there.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Local Law 152 of 2018, which DSNY spent more than a decade working with the City Council

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: prior to its enactment, required a reduction in the permitted capacity of putrescible and non-putrescible transfer stations in four historically overburdened community districts.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: By 50% in Brooklyn District 1, and by 33% in Queens District 12 and Bronx Districts 1 and 2.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: The law also allowed for certain exemptions to those reductions in permitted capacity for activities consistent with the city's sustainability goals, including the processing of recyclables and organic waste,

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: for diverting construction and demolition debris to beneficial use, and for facilities that export waste by rail.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Local Law 152 represented the culmination of years of advocacy and organizing that began decades ago, as the city began to close its own disposal facilities.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Today, the law has been fully implemented, and we have reduced not only permitted capacity, but also actual throughput and actual truck traffic.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: In these historically overburdened communities.

chapters.summary: Anderson says commercial waste zones under Local Law 199 will reduce truck traffic and emissions, projecting a 63% reduction in commercial waste truck traffic. He reports that six zones are fully operational and that pricing and service quality have improved.
chapters.title: Anderson discusses commercial waste zones and truck traffic reduction

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And the ongoing implementation of commercial waste zones will continue to reduce truck traffic in these neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: The commercial waste zone program is being implemented under Local Law 199 of 2019 to reform the commercial waste hauling system

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: by establishing new safety standards for workers in the industry,

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: improving service for businesses, increasing diversion rates, reducing vehicle miles traveled, as well as the harmful emissions that come from waste hauling trucks.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: When fully implemented, we expect that commercial waste zones will result in a 63% reduction in truck traffic associated with commercial waste collection, more than 18 million miles per year.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And the fiscal year 26 commercial waste zones annual report was released just two weeks ago, covering the expansion from just one initial zone to six fully operational zones as of the end of June of this year.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: DSNY has continued to strengthen the oversight framework, including monitoring awardee compliance,

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: collecting and reviewing required operational data, conducting enforcement activities, supporting worker safety initiatives, and engaging businesses and other stakeholders throughout every phase of implementation.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: There's a substantial amount of data and information in that report, including information on the 192,000 outreach activities we've conducted

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: by sanitation and our partners, 2,581 individual employee trainings conducted by carters.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: There's collection tonnage by zone and by stream, enforcement actions, and much, much more.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And I'll note that that data is all available in machine-readable, manipulatable format, not just a PDF.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: When Local Law 199 was enacted, some opponents projected that the program would cause massive disruption for businesses, drive up costs.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: and reduce the quality of service.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: To date, the opposite has been true.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Pricing and service quality have both improved, and the city's streets are both cleaner and safer as a result.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: We are proud of our implementation of this historic program, and we look forward to celebrating its full implementation at the end of next year.

chapters.summary: Anderson says DSNY contributed to the citywide racial equity plan and acknowledges inequities in service levels and neighborhood cleanliness. He commits to publishing neighborhood-level data on diversion, containerization, rat sightings, and vehicle miles traveled.
chapters.title: Anderson outlines racial equity plan and neighborhood data commitments

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: DSNY is also proud to have contributed to New York City's first citywide racial equity plan, mandated by voters in a 2022 ballot initiative.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: In this plan, we acknowledge that our operations are deeply connected with structural issues that affect New Yorkers of color.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And that our mission includes a responsibility to address inequities in service levels and neighborhood cleanliness.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: As we work to strengthen our efforts, we are committed to ensuring that our sanitation programs promote equity and serve all New Yorkers, especially those in historically underserved communities.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: In this report, we commit to continuously improving programs and service delivery to New Yorkers through ongoing evaluation of data analytics, stakeholder feedback, and operational enhancements that are responsive to community needs.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And in the coming years, we will publish neighborhood-level data sets to measure key outcomes around diversion, containerization, and commercial waste reform at the neighborhood level.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: These will include measures such as commercial and residential diversion rates, rat sightings, vehicle miles traveled, diversion participation, and we'll use those to identify disparities and target improvements.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: in our services.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: We'll also use this data to inform outreach, enforcement, and resource allocation.

chapters.summary: Anderson says DSNY agrees with moving aggressively on containerization but opposes Intro 30's requirement that all city agency facilities use Empire bins. He says city buildings already containerize waste and that adding Empire bins everywhere would divert resources from residential rollout.
chapters.title: Anderson testifies on Intro 30 city-owned building containerization

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Turning now to the legislation on today's agenda, Intro 30, sponsored by Councilmember Breu, would require sanitation in consultation with DCAS and DOE to create a program requiring city-owned buildings to dispose of waste in stationary on-street containers.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: DSNY agrees that we should move aggressively to containerize the city's trash.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And in fact, trash containerization has been required for all city agencies for nearly two years.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Trash containerization is imperative for New York City, but we must take a thoughtful and strategic approach that accounts for density and efficiency.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: This bill would require all city agency facilities, including small schools and offices, to use Empire bins, which may not be appropriate in all cases.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Moreover, all city buildings, as I said before, are already required to use some form of trash containerization, whether through tilt trucks, NYC bins, or off-street containerized collection.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: In developing the plan for the citywide rollout of Empire bins, we have focused on residential properties with 10 or more units not currently covered by our containerization requirements

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: to maximize the impact of our investments in getting trash bags off the sidewalk.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Empire bins now serve large residential buildings in West Harlem and are rolling out this fall in Brooklyn.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Community District 2, including downtown Brooklyn and Fort Greene.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And as the mayor announced this spring, we are on an aggressive timeline to achieve full trash containerization by 2031, faster than ever previously envisioned.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Adding Empire bins at every city facility as we roll out that program will divert resources from that important focus on residential trash and delay the full rollout.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: There are certainly some municipal buildings for which Empire bin service is appropriate, and we will pursue installation at the appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: We would be happy to continue conversations with the council as we expand our revolutionary trash containerization programs.

chapters.summary: Anderson says rechargeable batteries from powered mobility devices cause fires in trucks and facilities. He notes DSNY's special waste drop-off sites and safe events but says expanding collection would require additional resources and that battery manufacturers should bear more responsibility.
chapters.title: Anderson testifies on Intro 352 rechargeable battery disposal

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Intro 352 sponsored by Councilmember Nurse would require DSNY to develop a plan for ensuring proper disposal of rechargeable batteries from powered mobility devices.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: These batteries represent a major problem for sanitation and our partners, causing fires in our trucks and our facilities when they are improperly disposed of.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: DSNY currently offers services aligned with the spirit of this legislation.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: We recently expanded the operating hours of our special waste drop-off sites and now have one location in every borough that accepts rechargeable batteries, electronics, paint, and automotive products five days a week, Tuesday to Saturday, from 9 a.m.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: To 3 p.m.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Adding a second site in each borough and further expanding those hours would require substantial additional resources.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: The proposed bill also calls for DSNY to accept these items at any

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: or collection event organized by the department.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And while we do collect them at our safe events, one per borough per year, including one coming up this weekend on Staten Island,

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: it would be impractical to collect them at all department-sponsored events without additional funding or material support from the rechargeable battery industry.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And we do believe that battery manufacturers should be primarily responsible for the cost of collecting unwanted batteries and educating the public on safe use and disposal.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Many rechargeable batteries, but importantly, excluding those in e-mobility devices, are already covered by a New York State Extended Producer Responsibility and Retailer Take-Back Program.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: This law requires that all stores that sell rechargeable batteries or items that contain them must also collect them for recycling, and the cost of that program is borne by battery manufacturers.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: The state recently enacted legislation to expand this producer responsibility program to include e-mobility batteries.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Retailer take back and recycling of those items remains voluntary in the updated state law.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: We are currently working with DEC, FDNY, and the program's producer responsibility organization, the Battery Network, to ensure that the producer responsibility program implemented pursuant to this law provides for sufficiently safe

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: and convenient collection options for New York City residents, including by providing funding for city-operated collection sites and events.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: We appreciate the Council's

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: strong interest in this topic and we'll keep the council informed as these discussions progress.

chapters.summary: Anderson says DSNY has about 400 smart compost bins citywide but that utilization has declined since mandatory curbside composting began. He says DSNY cannot support Intro 401's requirement for 25 public organic waste receptacles per community district due to cost and service needs.
chapters.title: Anderson testifies on Intro 401 organic waste receptacles

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Intro 401 sponsored by Councilmember Ressler would require DSNY to install 25 public organic waste receptacles in every community district.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: We currently have a network of approximately 400 smart compost bins installed citywide.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And that program was established before the implementation of our nation-leading, mandatory, universal curbside composting program.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Which is our primary approach for providing composting service for New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Since the mandatory program has been fully implemented and we have actually been enforcing it, utilization of the smart compost bins has declined significantly.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And given this fact and the added cost to install and service the additional organic waste receptacles this bill would require, we cannot support this bill at this time.

chapters.summary: Anderson says DSNY already established an application process for shared Empire bins in Brooklyn District 2 for small and medium buildings. He looks forward to further discussions with the council on Intro 987.
chapters.title: Anderson testifies on Intro 987 shared on-street containers

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Intro 987, sponsored by Councilmember Abreu, would require DSNY to establish a process for block associations and nonprofits to request shared stationary on-street containers.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: We have already established an application process for shared Empire bins for small 1-9 unit and medium 10-30 unit buildings located in Brooklyn District 2 as we roll out this fall.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And we are actively seeking applicants to test that approach.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: We look forward to further discussions with the council about this legislation as we continue to implement our containerization program.

chapters.summary: Anderson says DSNY understands past litter basket removals were frustrating but that removals are now rare and a last resort. He says he has not removed a litter basket as commissioner and that DSNY recently began updating its litter basket inventory monthly.
chapters.title: Anderson testifies on Intro 1041 litter basket removals

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Lastly,

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Intro 1041, sponsored by Councilmember Hankerson, would change how the department considers litter basket removals.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: We understand that the department's past practice of removing chronically misused litter baskets was frustrating to elected officials and New Yorkers alike.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And today, several factors make such removals rare and, when exercised, the last possible resort.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: First, the department has the highest level of baseline funded litter basket service in recorded history, meaning that we are able to service every basket currently on the street more frequently all across the city.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Second, the department adjusts service levels more thoughtfully and proactively than in the past, changing the frequency and time of day of collection to best optimize service to a neighborhood's need.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Third, our network of community partners has grown in both size and scope, including bids, local mutual aid groups, and supplemental service providers.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And finally, thanks to action by the City Council several years ago, we have stronger enforcement tools to hold those who misuse our litter baskets for disposal of household and commercial waste accountable.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: In rare cases of clear recurring misuse that leads to consistent unmanageable overflow, sanitation may determine that a basket must be removed or relocated.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Any such removals are subject to my own personal review, and it is an action that I do not take lightly.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And in fact, we have not yet...

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Removed a Lear basket since I have been commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: But it is critical that we retain this tool

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: as an option of last resort to address chronic misuse and improper disposal that affects our city's neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And on reporting, I'm happy to say that we recently began updating the litter basket inventory posted on open data on a monthly rather than quarterly basis.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And I'd be happy to discuss with you further reporting, transparency, and accountability with the council.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So thank you for the opportunity to testify on these topics today, and we are happy to answer your questions.

chapters.title: Sanchez asks about number of private and municipal transfer stations

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: So just let's start with some general oversight.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: How many private waste transfer stations are there in New York City?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Hold on.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: There are...

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: It looks like about 16 putrescible waste transfer stations and another, I would say, roughly 21 non-putrescible waste transfer stations.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And how many municipal waste transfer stations are there in New York City?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: And can you also give us the breakdown?

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks how DSNY implemented the required permitted capacity reductions between 2019 and 2020. Anderson explains that DSNY started with existing permitted capacity, removed exempted material such as organics and demonstrated recycling, then applied the required percentage reduction.
chapters.title: Sanchez questions capacity reduction implementation and exemptions

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And can you walk us through how the required permitted capacity reductions of the waste equity law were implemented by DSNY in each of the four designated districts between 2019 and 2020?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Yeah, so the permitted capacity reductions, we started with the existing permitted capacity.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: We took out any exempted material, so that was...

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: A certain amount could be set aside for organic waste processing.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: We gave, and this was all laid out in Local Law 152, there was credit for demonstrated recyclables processing.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So if you were taking in, let's say, 100 tons a day of single stream recycling or paper recycling, that got set aside as an exemption.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And for C&D transfer stations, we set aside any actual demonstrated recycling that they were doing.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Whatever permitted capacity was left got reduced by the percentage set forth in Local Law 152.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: So analysis of the waste equity law data shows that none of the four designated CDs have achieved 100% compliance with the law's reduction.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Specifically looking at the waste equity data, BK1 required 50%, but is only at 35.8% overall reduction, including both stations.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Similarly, the 33% reduction, MBX1, is only down.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: to 14.8%, BX2 is down to 21%, and Queens 12 is down to 23.9%.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Were any required reductions exempted in any of the four CDs?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And if so, which exemptions were used and for which facilities?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So the way that the exemptions are applied under local law 152 is that those are applied first prior to the reduction in permitted capacity.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And then the remaining amount after the exemptions is what's reduced by the either 33% or 50% based on the community district.

chapters.summary: Sanchez notes that none of the four designated districts achieved full compliance and asks whether reductions targeted unused capacity. Anderson says it was a mix and that actual throughput decreased for some facilities.
chapters.title: Sanchez probes compliance gaps and unused capacity

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And have capacity reductions targeted mostly unused capacity at waste transfer stations?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: It's a mix of both.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: There are, as I said in my testimony, there were actual reductions in throughput as a result of the implementation of this law.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So there was...

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Real tangible capacity that had been used prior to the implementation of local 152 that can no longer be used.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: So can you explain to us what challenges that the department has faced implementing the law and the law's reduction requirements, what more challenges have been faced, and what can be done to ensure that

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: total compliance is achieved.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So we've achieved total compliance with the law as it was written and enacted by the city council and as was laid out in the environmental review that we did ahead of the law's passage.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So from our perspective, we have implemented that law.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: That doesn't mean that we have

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: stopped working toward additional waste equity.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And I think the commercial waste zones program is a great example of that.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Not only will a commercial waste zones program reduce truck traffic citywide, but it will reduce truck traffic in particular in neighborhoods that host waste transfer stations, commercial

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: parting hubs of operations and other waste related facilities.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And so, you know, we have seen and will continue to see truck traffic reduce in those neighborhoods as we implement that program.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks Anderson to explain exemptions in more detail. Anderson uses the IWS transfer station in Bronx Community District 1 as an example, explaining how recycling capacity was set aside before the 33% reduction and added back afterward.
chapters.title: Sanchez asks about exemption mechanics and specific facilities

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: So you said we've hit all of the all of the reduction markers, but

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Can you explain again?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: So first you took out all the exemptions.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Can you talk to us about what these exemptions were and what that means to the actual number in reduction that we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Yeah, so the law required us to go transfer station by transfer station and take the existing permitted capacity.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Then take any exemptions that were set forth in the law very explicitly Remove those from the existing permitted capacity

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Take the reduction as a percentage basis and then add back the exempted permit So if you take and I'm just going to use an example here to make it more concrete

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: But if you take, let's say, the action environmental, now it's IWS, transfer station in Bronx Community District 1, their initial permitted capacity was 2999.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Their new permitted capacity was 2101.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: The reason that that's not

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: 1999 or 2000 depending on how you round is because they had existing recyclable materials that they were processing through that facility demonstrated in previous

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: transfer station reports to sanitation and to DEC and so under local law 152 that

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: that amount of recycling, the average amount of recycling, I think it was a, I think a one year, maybe two year look back, was set aside prior to the 33% reduction being applied and then added back after the 33% reduction.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Okay, seems.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And so when you go facility by facility,

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: There are exemptions for many, not all, of the facilities that had reductions taken.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: So talking about those facilities, I do want to highlight waste management in DX1 and in BK1.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: It doesn't look like they had, from the data that we have, that there have been any reductions whatsoever there.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And so can you help explain why these facilities didn't go through any required capacity reductions, especially when there's no reported capacity reserves at these stations for organics?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: What other exemptions did they receive?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Yeah, so there's an exemption in Local 152 for any facility that exports the majority of its waste by rail, and both of those waste management facilities export nearly all of their waste by rail.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Some facilities like the Metropolitan Transportation and BX2 actually received capacity increases in 2025.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Why was that?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Yeah, so again, there was a provision in Local 152 that allows for facilities that want to add additional capacity for organics processing or for recyclable material processing to take a one-time

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: credit for that investment in new processing infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And so they applied for and received that one-time credit.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And that's all that process is laid out in local law 152 as well.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks why the four designated environmental justice districts were not prioritized for containerization pilots. Anderson says Bronx Community District 2 is first on next year's list and that every district will have full containerization by 2031.
chapters.title: Sanchez questions containerization prioritization in EJ districts

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And I have more questions, but I'm going to make sure that we turn it over to my colleague really quickly.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: But I'm just curious.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: So you mentioned a lot of

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: the additional work that you have been doing in terms of the supplemental work to the waste equity law.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: I'm talking about containerization, talking about all these advancements.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: But the thing that I find really curious is that out of all of the districts that we mentioned, none of those districts outside of now Bronx 2, CD2,

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: are the start of the containerization pilot?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Were any a part of any of these programs?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And I'm curious, why weren't these districts prioritized over other districts that didn't need it as much as we did?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Bronx 2 is first on the list for next year, so I think we're coming that way.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Yes, but my question is, is there a reason why these four districts that we had outlined that we understood, why weren't they the number one priorities for these containerization pilots, for any of these pilots that are coming out,

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: rather than other districts that aren't?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: The top of this list that have been dealing with these burdens that these other communities haven't, but are getting the nice things before us.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: I would say the fact that one of those districts is one of the first three districts to receive Empire bins is a sign that we are in

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: in fact, doing exactly what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Yes, but also I don't think we're answering the question of like why those other districts were chosen.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And also it's one out of I think we have the nine or 10 outlined already.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And out of those, only one are in these top EJ districts and overburdened communities.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And so curious why there hasn't been a bigger push for any of these other places to be put in as well.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So the great news is that every district in New York City will have full trash containerization by the end of 2031.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So we are coming for every district citywide.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: As we discussed in previous hearings, the methodology for selecting the next six districts after Manhattan Community District 9, West Harlem, and Brooklyn Community District 2 was, one, we wanted to have districts in each of the five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So we are adding two districts in the Bronx, one in Manhattan, one in Queens, one in Brooklyn, one in Staten Island.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Second, we wanted to test this in a variety of different sort of geographic and density use cases.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So, you know, we're doing this, we're rolling out in Bronx 5, for example, which will be the hilliest district that we've ever put Empire bins in.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: We're coming to Bronx Community District 2, which, as you've highlighted, I think has, you know, many of the equity and socioeconomic concerns that we're trying to address through much of this work.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: We're going to Queens.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: West 2, which is the fastest growing neighborhood in the United States at this moment.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So I think we picked districts based on a bunch of different criteria.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Equity was certainly one of them.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And I think the fact that we're coming to Bronx District 2 is a marker of that.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Can we get a commitment from the admin that the next districts after these six will be the remaining three environmental community districts that are waiting to have some justice?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: We'll certainly take a look at it.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: We will follow back up on that.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Side staffed question.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Councilmember Hankerson, and also before we, we are, have been greatly joined by Councilmember Ressler.

chapters.summary: Council Member Hankerson asks when DSNY stopped removing litter baskets due to illegal dumping. Anderson says he ended the practice when he became commissioner in March 2026 and that DSNY now relocates rather than removes baskets.
chapters.title: Hankerson asks when DSNY halted litter basket removals

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Councilmember Hankerson, the floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: I'm going to move relatively quickly through my questions.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: When did the department halt the practice of removing trash bins on the basis of illegal dumping?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So I became commissioner on March 30th, 2026.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And one of the first things I said to my team was absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: We are not doing that anymore.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Does the agency still remove baskets, but for other reasons aside from illegal dumping?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: In general, no.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: What we will sometimes do is, and a lot of this happens in close collaboration with city council members, we'll move baskets from, you know, if there's four corners at an intersection, we'll move it from one corner.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: corner to another based on a concern from a resident or a business owner or the location of a bus stop, maybe that gets moved, something like that.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So we certainly do relocate them, but we don't generally remove them.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: How often do you collaborate with council members to make that decision?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: All the time, on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: No one's called me.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: I think you know how to get in touch with us.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So if you want us to come out and talk about your litter baskets, we're happy to do so anytime.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: I'd love for you all to get in touch with me as well.

chapters.summary: Hankerson asks how DSNY determines litter basket placement. Anderson cites bus routes, subway stations, commercial corridors, and BID areas, and Hankerson points to a disparity between Metropolitan Avenue and Archer Avenue in Queens.
chapters.title: Hankerson questions litter basket placement criteria and disparities

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: So how does the agency determine where litter baskets are placed?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: There's a number of factors that go into it.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: We look at things like bus routes.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: We look at things like subway stations.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Litter baskets, because they are predominantly for the kind of trash that you have when you're walking around, a coffee cup, a water bottle, a sandwich wrapper,

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: we predominantly put them in places along commercial corridors because that's where you have the most pedestrians and the most people sort of carrying that material.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And then we look at other factors like where there are bids, there are more litter baskets because the bids, in some cases, purchase those litter baskets themselves.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So in bid areas, we have a much higher concentration.

utterances.text: I'm glad you said that.

utterances.text: If we can look into it before the walkthrough, so that's not actually in my district, but that station is serviced or used by folks in my district.

chapters.title: Hankerson asks about basket types and council funding

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: hour after hour it just doesn't really make sense how do you determine the type of litter basket that's placed on a corner

utterances.text: There's a couple different factors we take into account.

utterances.text: One, some council members tell us they prefer a certain type of litter basket, and if they do that, then we try to honor that preference.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson

utterances.text: But generally, you know, we're trying to achieve a consistent look and feel across a given corridor.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: So if a member allocates money towards the purchase of litter baskets, do they have more of a say as to where those litter baskets go, or is that still fully determined by DSNY?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Every council member can provide input on where the litter baskets go.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: When they're buying litter baskets, sure, we have a conversation about where would you like the, again, let's use the number 250, but it could be 10, 20, 30, 40.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: We have a conversation with that member's office around where do you want these specific litter baskets to go?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Do you want to replace?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Older litter baskets?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Do you want to try to fill in gaps in the litter basket network?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So we have that conversation with every- I have a follow up to that, but I'm running out of time.

chapters.summary: Hankerson asks whether truck operators must report missing litter baskets. Anderson says workers should report missing baskets and that DSNY conducts quarterly physical inventories of about 25,049 approved locations, finding about 3,300 missing baskets.
chapters.title: Hankerson asks about reporting missing baskets and inventory

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: I'm going to try and get through these last two, if that's okay, Mr.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Chair.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Are truck operators mandated to report if a litter basket is removed off of their route?

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Let's say sanitation, because I've been told by some of your chiefs that sometimes baskets are removed by residents or businesses and not actually the department.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: So is a truck operator mandated to report if a basket is not there that they typically see?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Yeah, so the sanitation workers, whether they're on.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Curbside collection service or litter basket collection service should be reporting to us.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: We also, on a quarterly basis, do a full litter basket inventory.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So the list.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: list of litter basket locations that we have approved right now, I think is like 25,049.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And we will send officers out and do a physical inventory of every single approved location and determine, is there a litter basket on site?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: What kind of litter basket?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Is it damaged?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Is it broken?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Does it need to be replaced?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And so we go through that process on a quarterly basis.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: That's how right now we know there are about 3,300 missing litter baskets across New York City.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And we are in the process right now of trying to replace every single one of those missing litter baskets.

chapters.summary: Hankerson asks what enforcement tools DSNY uses for illegal dumping. Anderson says dumping from a vehicle carries a $4,000 ticket, substantial dumping carries a $75,000 ticket, and improper household or commercial waste near a litter basket carries a $75 ticket.
chapters.title: Hankerson questions enforcement tools for illegal dumping

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Final question.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: What are the enforcement tools used by the agency to address illegal dumping?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So, and I'll just, as a point of clarification, when we talk about illegal dumping, we mean dumping from a vehicle.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: That's typically not the kind of issues we have around litter baskets.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: But the...

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to have to disagree with you.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: In my district, I've seen folks pull up to a litter basket in a vehicle, a van, and dump.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: And, you know, obviously in talking with members of the department, you know, they'll say, oh, it's household trash.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: But I'm like, no, it's not always household trash.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Sometimes it is someone just taking, whether it's debris from a construction site or whatever, and dumping it on a corner at a litter basket.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: So that's why I say it that way.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Yeah, and I think that's an important distinction, and every situation is different.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: At the end of the day, it's a $4,000 ticket.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: If you dump a substantial amount of material from a vehicle, it's a $75,000.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: $1 ticket if you improperly dispose of household or commercial waste near a litter basket.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And so, you know, in general, we, when it's that kind of household trash near a litter basket, we'll issue the $75 ticket.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: If we see any identifying information, if we have a corner store that has a security camera and can tell us it came from this house or it came from this other business, we can issue a ticket based on that because there's a presumption of responsibility there.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Chair Sanchez thanks Council Member Hankerson and notes that Council Member Maloney has joined. He then turns the floor over to Council Member Carl Wilson.
chapters.title: Sanchez thanks Hankerson and turns to Wilson

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Councilmember Hankerson.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: I want to flag that we've also been joined by the amazing Councilmember Maloney.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And I would now like to turn it over to Councilmember Wilson.

chapters.summary: Council Member Wilson asks about wait times for replacing missing litter baskets after a 311 call. Anderson says wait times vary, that DSNY is systematically replacing baskets, and that the goal is to replace every identified missing basket by the end of the calendar year.
chapters.title: Wilson asks about litter basket replacement wait times

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: My colleague from Queens asked a lot of my questions, so may not use the whole time.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Just on the replacements of the baskets, you said you buy a few hundred a year.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: A few hundred of the better bins.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Of the better bins.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: So what is the wait time like on a replacement right now?

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: If someone makes a 311 call, they're missing one here.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: How long does it take?

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: For a new basket to go out to the corner?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Yes, the wait time, I would say, varies because we're trying to replace baskets pretty systematically.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: You know, we right now actually just got an update from my team that Councilmember Williams baskets are in the process of being replaced.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So some of those that may have been missing and identified in that viral video are in the process of being replaced as we get litter baskets in from our vendor.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So, you know, if it's a 311 complaint, it might be a few weeks or even a month or two before they're replaced if we had just done a big replacement cycle in that district because we want to try to sort of fill all the holes.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Our goal is by the end of this calendar year to have replaced every litter basket that we've identified as

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: as an approved location that is missing, and then have a sort of good baseline for being able to replace litter baskets on a more consistent basis going forward.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: The last administration, just to be frank, did not emphasize replacing missing litter baskets.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: They were much more focused on buying fewer of the nicer, better bin litter baskets,

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: rather than many, many more of the utilitarian green wire litter basket that we all know and love.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: We are trying to balance those two things by buying more of the green wire litter baskets in order to be able to just fill the holes that we know are out there.

chapters.summary: Wilson asks whether the Better Bin design is working given broken parts. Anderson says Better Bins have more parts that can break, but DSNY tries to replace individual parts rather than remove the whole basket, and that they work better in some neighborhoods than others.
chapters.title: Wilson questions Better Bin design and maintenance

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: And for the better bins, is the design...

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: How's the design working?

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Because I feel like I walk around my district and I see them in so many different states.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: You know, the door is ripped off, the piece is missing off the top.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: And does that contribute to a removal?

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: And is the design of the Better Bin working out?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So I would say the Better Bins are, they have more parts to them.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So there's more things that could break.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: A standard green wire litter basket has exactly one part, and so it either works or it doesn't.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: But with the Better Bins, if the top is missing, the great news is it still functions as a litter basket.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: It just doesn't look whole.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So we do try to replace individual parts rather than remove the entire basket just because the top is missing.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: I will say they work well in some neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: They don't work well in others.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: They don't work well in places where you have a lot of graffiti and stickers because they act as a magnet for those graffiti and stickers.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And so we try to work with council members to say, here are the pros and cons of this basket versus a green wire litter basket and try to identify the best one for their neighborhood.

chapters.summary: Wilson asks whether DSNY prioritizes basket replacements in areas without community partners. Anderson says BIDs often replace their own baskets, while DSNY conducts quarterly inventories and is replacing every approved missing basket; he offers to discuss additional locations.
chapters.title: Wilson asks about prioritizing replacements in areas without partners

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: And in terms of when you're replacing, you mentioned a lot of the community partners that you have and work with, but I don't know that this is sort of anecdotal, but

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: I feel like where I don't have a community partner is where I'm missing a lot of my bins.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: So do you prioritize your replacements maybe in those areas that don't have a partner?

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: But like, for instance, in Chelsea, south of Penn Station, tremendous foot traffic.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: But that's where I'm missing like a ton of.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: That's where I get complaints a lot about baskets being missed.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: And there's no community partner there to report on that and to clean them so that they could really use them.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: So how does that factor into when you're looking at where to replace, target your replacement?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Yeah, so where there are bids that own and install their own litter baskets, those are obviously getting replaced by the bids.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So there's a...

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Much more just sort of attention to those baskets.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And they may even have dozens of extra baskets in inventory ready to go out if something gets damaged or stolen.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Where there are baskets that are only serviced by us and only managed by us, again, it goes

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: through this process of every quarter we do a full inventory of all of our litter baskets and we are in the process now of replacing every single approved litter basket location that does not currently have a basket.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: There may be places in the area that you're talking about that are not currently approved for a litter basket and so they're

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: It's not technically missing because it wasn't supposed to be there.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: If there are places where you think there should be additional litter baskets, we're certainly happy to have that conversation.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: I did send you all a letter about those, so I'd love to know which of those are approved.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: I have a draft response to that letter sitting in my inbox right now.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.
