utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: That's all for me.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks for exact numbers of litter baskets removed due to misuse in 2025 and 2026. Anderson says DSNY does not have those numbers and that the practice largely ended around the end of the de Blasio administration.
chapters.title: Sanchez asks for litter basket removal numbers for misuse

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember Wilson.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And just staying on this topic real quick, do we have an exact number of how many litter baskets the department removed due to misuse, so depositing household or commercial refuse or liquid waste in baskets

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: in 2025, as well as how many it's removed in 2026 for those same reasons?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: We don't have those numbers.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And in large part, this practice was, in effect, more than 10 years ago.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And, you know, sometime around the end of the de Blasio administration, the decision was made by previous commissioners to cease that practice.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So if you go back in.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: News reports, for example, there was a number of baskets removed in central Harlem at one point, I think around 2017, 2018.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And that caused prior administrations to really rethink if this is the right approach.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: There were also even going back further to 2013, 2014.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: in parts of Ridgewood along specifically Fresh Pond Road.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: I know that there was a lot of consternation around removed litter baskets.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And so sometime around the end of the de Blasio administration, the practice from wide scale removals to much more targeted removals was made.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And, you know, I know that the number of baskets removed has fallen off pretty substantially since then.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks why 311 complaints take over a month while social media complaints seem to get immediate responses. Anderson says DSNY treats complaints the same and directs people to 311, and Sanchez urges residents to file 311 requests.
chapters.title: Sanchez questions 311 response times versus social media complaints

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: On my final question about the wasteland basket.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: So according to 311, it usually takes over a month to get a response as to fulfilling a trash basket request.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: However, many of my constituents included, and I know many of my colleagues feel that

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: If you post a cool, fun social media video, you get a response almost immediately.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Can you explain to us why there's such a disparity in the response times from 311 complaints to potential social media complaints and how you have been handling these?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Random social media complaints that seem to get fulfilled right away.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: I would be interested to know which of the random social media complaints you're referring to, because a lot of people add us on social media and we treat every complaint the same.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Do you tell them to all file a 311 complaint?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: We often, I mean, our standard response, if you send us something on Twitter, Instagram, I don't know that we actively monitor customer complaints on TikTok.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: but we do have a TikTok.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: You know, if you send us a complaint, our first response is to give you the link to the 311 and say, please file a 311.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So that's where we'd like all New Yorkers to go, because then we can track how quickly our officers are responding, what their response is, and the level of satisfaction that customers have with that response.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Well, you've heard it here first, ladies and gentlemen.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Social media is not 311.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Please put in your 311 request for your trash bins, your litter request.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: We are begging you.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: 311, and then send us your 311 complaint number.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And I'll also add, if I may.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: That I think sanitation is probably one of the only agencies that, and it's not universal, but in many cases will call back the 311 caller or online request submitter, whatever you call that.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So if you do provide your contact information, our officers will give you a call and follow up.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: It may not be the outcome that you want, but at least they'll talk you through why the decision was made the way it was.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: I can confirm they will call you at any time to confirm.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Sometimes early in the morning.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Very early in the morning.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: But again, New Yorkers, 311, it's the way to get things done, not social media.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks how to access exemptions granted to companies in environmental justice districts. Anderson agrees to provide a copy and discusses the one capacity increase at the Metropolitan Transfer Station in Bronx Community District 2 for organics processing.
chapters.title: Sanchez requests exemption data and asks about capacity increases

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Okay, going back to our questions before we turn it over to Councilmember Ressler.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: So I want to go over.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Back to these exemptions, is there a way that we can get a copy of where we can access the exemptions that have been given to companies in the EJ districts?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Or where would we be able to find, you know, in order to make sure that we have the best data as well, so that we're not being like, you're not fulfilling your goals.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: If we don't have the exemptions that they've been granted, then to us it looks like you haven't been fulfilling the goals.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: So is there a way that we can get provided a copy of that, or where can we find that?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Sure, we can provide you a copy of that.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Has the department allowed any capacity increases in any over-concentrated districts?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And if so, what was the basis for each of the permitted increases?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Yeah, so the one increase that I can recall is the one that you referred to earlier, Metropolitan Transfer Station at 287 Halleck Street in Bronx 2.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And that was an increase because they...

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Added 111 tons per day of capacity to process organic waste.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: So have there been any incidents since the...

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Just a note, the law does prohibit them from increasing their permanent capacity over what their permanent capacity was prior to the implementation of Local Law 152.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So it was 825, it went to 553, and then came up to 664.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Great.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks whether throughput ever exceeded 90% of permitted capacity and whether it was reported. Anderson says he is not aware of specific instances but will check; he attributes citywide throughput decrease partly to Local Law 152 shifting waste out of the city.
chapters.title: Sanchez asks about throughput exceeding 90% and citywide decrease

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Has there, I want to flag, this also was in 2018.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: This hasn't been.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: and been 10 years ago, it seems like it was an entire lifetime.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Having said that, have there been any incidents since this lifetime ago where the law was implemented where throughput at any of the solid waste transfer stations exceeded 90% of the total permitted capacity for such transfer stations?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And if this had happened, were these instances reported to the council and the mayor?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Where throughput exceeded 90% of the permitted capacity.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: I'm not aware of specific instances, but we can certainly take a look at that.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Overall city throughput has decreased since 2019.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Can you help us understand what explains this trend?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Well, one, I think the implementation of Local Law 152 reduced overall citywide throughput because the majority of transfer stations were located in districts that were covered by Local Law 152.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So when you reduce the permitted capacity citywide, you have to send that waste elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So more of that waste is going either up to Westchester County or into New Jersey in places that aren't regulated by the Department of Sanitation.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: I think there's also a part of it that could be related to just waste reduction overall.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: We'll say because we have not fully implemented commercial waste zones, we don't have good historical data on the amount of waste that our businesses are generating.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And so, you know, that's speculation at this point.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Once we have commercial waste zones fully implemented at the end of 2027, we will have very robust data on where the waste is being generated, where it's going, and what kind of waste it is.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And I encourage you to look at the full data set that we posted along with the commercial waste zones annual report, which has a lot of data in it.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Awesome.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And then when looking at this data, we see that the throughput decreased primarily in non-designated CDs, while the throughput remained the same in the four designated CDs since 2019.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Could you also help us explain that trend?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: don't necessarily know that I'm seeing the same trend, but we'd be happy to dig into the data with you.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Okay, that'd be great.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: We would really love to make sure that we're all on the same page there.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks about truck traffic effects in designated districts and about Local Laws 145 and 199. Anderson says DSNY cannot measure actual truck traffic yet but modeling predicted reductions, and that Local Law 145 emissions retrofits and commercial waste zones are expected to reduce vehicle miles traveled.
chapters.title: Sanchez questions truck traffic impacts of Local Laws 145 and 199

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: What were the law effects on truck traffic in the designated commercial districts?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Community districts?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Commercial districts.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: What a day.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Community districts.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And did we see truck traffic decrease?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: I know you spoke about it earlier, but if you could go into a little more detail.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So I don't think we're able to measure the actual decrease in truck traffic because we don't have data on how many trucks there are and where until commercial waste zones is fully implemented.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: We did quite a bit of modeling as a part of the environmental assessment that was done prior to the passage of Local Law 152.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And what we...

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: anticipated as part of that environmental assessment was a substantial decrease in truck traffic in those districts.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: We have seen that actual throughput has decreased by about the amount we expected in that environmental review.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So I would think that the truck traffic reduction has been approximately what we expected.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Even though we can't answer about

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: the waste equity law.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: I'm curious if you've done any research or insight if local law 199 of 2019 had any impact on truck traffic thus far.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And what about local law 145, if that had any impact on the waste equity laws implementation with truck emissions?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So for local law 145, which goes back to 2013, that was the law that required emissions retrofits for all waste hauling vehicles.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: That law has been fully implemented.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: The last of the waivers under that law expired several years ago.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So I think that has had a real impact on the particulate matter emissions from those commercial waste hauling vehicles.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: I don't have a rigorous analysis of that in front of me, but that's something that I think just the implementation of that law over several thousand vehicles has had a real impact.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: For local law 199,

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: We are and we do publish to the like decimal point the amount of

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: vehicle miles traveled associated with commercial waste zones operations.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Because we only have six zones fully implemented at the end of the fiscal year, and some of those commercial waste zones were implemented partially throughout the fiscal year,

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: what we're able to do is model out based on those first six zones where we expect to be at the end of the full 20 zone implementation.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And we are pretty much on track for that 18 million vehicle miles traveled reduction that we anticipated in 2018.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks what other solutions DSNY has considered to decrease truck traffic in the four designated districts. Anderson says commercial waste zones are the most effective tool and that relocating transfer capacity would require rezoning industrial areas or building new transfer stations.
chapters.title: Sanchez asks about solutions to decrease truck traffic in designated CDs

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Particularly in the four designated CDs, has DSNY considered any other solutions to decrease truck traffic?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: We've, you know, I think the implementation of commercial waste zones is the most effective tool that we can use to reduce truck traffic.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: You know, I think absent rezoning new parts of the city for industrial uses and opening new transfer stations in those rezoned places,

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: I think it will be very difficult to meaningfully relocate transfer station capacity out of those four districts and into other parts of the city.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: The best we could do is just shift the burden elsewhere onto environmental justice neighborhoods outside of New York City.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And I don't know that that's necessarily a great outcome, but that's certainly what Local Law 152 has done.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Not the best outcome.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Not everyone wants stuff in other EJ zones, but if it's not in the Bronx, it's good to me.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Actually, I will turn it over to Councilmember Ressler.

chapters.summary: Council Member Lincoln Restler thanks Chair Sanchez and praises DSNY leadership and local operations. He notes that he sees DSNY does not support his bill, Intro 401 on public organic waste receptacles.
chapters.title: Restler praises DSNY and introduces concerns with Intro 401

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thanks so much, Chair Sanchez.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Really appreciate your leadership and hosting this hearing today and hearing our legislation.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And Commissioner, it is always good to see you.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I have to say I am very happy that we have commercial waste zones coming to Community Board 1.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We have Empire Bins coming to Community Board 2.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I just had a great meeting with Chief Latera, who's helping to make all the good things happen on the ground.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We did ASP blitzes this week and last week in Borum Hill.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: There's just a lot of good stuff.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And I consistently have a really positive experience with whoever I'm dealing with at the Department of Sanitation.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And I really appreciate that we've just had...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I think going back since the beginning of the de Blasio administration, really consistently great leadership from the agency, and I am thrilled that you're in this role and looking forward to continuing to work closely with you and your team.

chapters.summary: Restler explains that Intro 401 aims to place compost receptacles in every community district for on-the-go food scraps. Anderson says smart compost bin utilization dropped 42% from FY25 to FY26 and that DSNY would rather invest in education and outreach.
chapters.title: Restler questions compost receptacles and smart bin utilization

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I see that you don't like my bill.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So I said all the nice things first.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: You might want to take back those compliments.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Yeah, I know.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Well, we'll see how the conversation goes.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So appreciate that the smart compost bins were kind of created in a different moment before we had mandatory composting fully in place.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And our legislation is, I think, rightly ambitious in trying to set a sizable number of

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: compost receptacles around every community district because there are times when you're having lunch in a park or having lunch at a city council hearing and you need a compost receptacle for your excess food.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Do you think that a smaller number of

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Compost receptacles per community district could make sense if 25 is too big a number.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: I think that, and if you look at the utilization of our smart compost bins, FY25, and this is all in our zero waste report, which came out also on September 30th, the same day as our commercial waste zones annual report, big day for annual reports in sanitation.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: FY25, almost 1.1 million unlocks.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: FY26, 0.6 million unlocks, 42% reduction in utilization over that one year.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And keep in mind, we have only very recently been really focusing on enforcement for mandatory organics.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: I, for example, used to use a smart bin until my building got a ticket for not having a compost bin.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And then they got a compost bin, and now I just use my building's compost bin.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So I just, I don't think that that's an investment that necessarily makes sense at this time.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: I think if there is a pot of money that we are going to invest in composting in New York City, it's probably better spent on education and outreach

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: rather than providing additional bins for folks because we will come to every building in New York City once a week and pick it up from the front of your building.

chapters.summary: Restler raises concerns about the stability of compost drop-off sites at farmers markets and about large buildings with trash chutes not setting up composting. Anderson agrees access for large buildings is important and encourages residents to call 311 if their building lacks a brown bin.
chapters.title: Restler asks about compost drop-off sites and large building composting

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: You know, our legislation, the idea was to make composting convenient on street corners for the times where it's not your household waste.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: But, you know, as I think during your brief sojourn up to Albany, we, you know, really struggled here when Grow NYC.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Refused to continue to operate compost drop-offs at their farmers markets.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: You know, at the farmers markets in my community, in McCarran Park and McGolrick Park, McGolrick is with Big Reuse, McCarran, well, I think Big Reuse is taking over McCarran too, that was a growing YC market.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: As examples, we still have huge numbers of people that come every single week to drop their compost off.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And so,

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I'm concerned that we still need locations for people to be able to take their compost, whether it's household or otherwise.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We've gotten a lot of complaints from larger buildings that have trash chutes and where they're not having composting set up in the buildings.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Maybe it's just the scale of the buildings are challenging for...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: The building management staff to handle the compost.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Are you concerned about, I guess there's a couple questions there.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: One, are you concerned about the full adoption of composting, especially in larger buildings where the operations are a bit more involved?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And then secondly, are you concerned about

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: the stability of the compost drop-off sites we have across the city.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And do you believe that they serve an essential role in kind of achieving our compost goals?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So thank you for those questions.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And it's two very different questions.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Fully agree with you on access to.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Convenient composting for apartment building residents, particularly in larger buildings.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And that's a place where we are doing a lot of enforcement already.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: If there are residents out there whose buildings do not have a brown bin and are not setting a brown bin out for collection,

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Call 311, let us know.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: We'll do outreach first, and then we will write tickets, and we will not stop.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And that's where, in addition, I think the outreach and education is really valuable to teach people how easy it is to compost in their own apartment.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: When my wife and I first started composting, she was not a fan.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And she was just like, why do we need four different trash cans?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Now we were just at my in-laws house in Pennsylvania where they don't compost.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And she literally was looking around my mother-in-law's kitchen for a place to put the eggshells.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And so, and we live in a high rise apartment in Long Island City.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So, you know, it is easy for apartment residents to compost.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: If you know how to do it, and if you have some easy tips, if we had more resources to be able to do that outreach and education, I think that's where the investment is really meaningful.

chapters.summary: Restler and Anderson discuss the value of community compost drop-offs with dedicated composters. Anderson says community composting baseline funds were eliminated in 2023 and that drop-offs serve a different purpose than smart bins; Restler says he will continue pushing for tailored compost receptacles.
chapters.title: Restler and Anderson discuss community composting funding and drop-off vs smart bins

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: If I can continue going, because I know his clock has run out.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Okay, no one's saying no.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: On the drop-off side, I think the kinds of drop-offs that you're talking about are very different than the organic waste receptacles that the bill calls for.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Those are drop-offs where you have a dedicated community composter standing next to the bin, helping people

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: feel good about what they're doing and helping people understand that it's going to be turned into compost at a local community garden or at a community composting facility and go back to

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: their local parks and gardens and whatever.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And I think that's all great stuff.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: When the community composting baseline funds were eliminated from the budget in November 2023, that was a massive, massive.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Change to the way that we approach composting in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And I have said before, I would love to have those baseline funds back in the budget so that we don't have to have this ongoing sort of tit for tat on whether composting is getting funded every year.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: I don't think that the people who are showing up at the green markets looking to have that interaction with the community composter and have that sort of

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: you know, local sort of circular economy for their compost would necessarily

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: the same way about using an organic waste receptacle like a smart bin that is collected by sanitation, goes to one of our industrial scale processing facilities, either a compost facility or anaerobic digestion.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So I don't think it's all the same.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I think you've made all very good points.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And I think that

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I still feel that in super high-trafficked areas, in big parks like McCarran Park or Borough Hall, having a compost receptacle, having one of these compost smart bins still has value.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So I'd love to continue the conversation if there's a much more tailored approach that you think could make sense.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: It doesn't sound like you think it does, but I will push you anyway.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And I will say lastly, I also take credit for converting my wife into a compost enthusiast as well.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: I'm sure our wives will be thrilled that we're discussing them here.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: I was just going to say blessings to both of your wives.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: On behalf of the city of New York, thank you.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks whether more public compost bins in parks could educate residents about composting. Anderson says bins could help but that without baseline funding for education and outreach, access alone is not the most effective investment.
chapters.title: Sanchez asks whether public compost bins can serve as education

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: On this topic of public composting, I am curious as to what the definition of education is.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And just to piggyback off of what Councilmember Resser was saying, having more of these public compost bins,

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: especially in places like these parks, wouldn't that part of education show how easy composting is and how, you know, getting more people to be able to compost, especially when they're doing things in the park like barbecuing and, you know, bringing food.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Dominican, so we bring a lot of different food and being able to be able to compost all of that when it's not eaten or whatever.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Wouldn't that be a part of the education that would be able to show how easy it is to truly compost?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: I think it could be, but I think there's some, you know, pretty...

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: As we've discussed before, we don't have very much in the way of baseline funding for education and outreach around our zero waste programs and our recycling and composting programs.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And so, you know, I think that could contribute.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: But if we're not teaching people about why they should compost or how they can compost, I think giving them access to a bin isn't necessarily the most effective thing that we can do.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So, you know.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Again, to roll out the bill as it's been introduced, we're looking at millions of dollars in expense money to purchase additional bins and install them.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And I think that money could better be spent on maybe on community composters going out into neighborhoods and teaching people about why they should compost.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: So what you're saying is we need baseline funding in order to convert more wives and husbands to composters.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: I would love that.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks how DSNY plans to implement the racial equity plan's strategies on distributing waste transfer operations and using solid waste contracts. Anderson says DSNY is committed to using marine transfer stations for commercial waste after commercial waste zones are fully implemented.
chapters.title: Sanchez questions racial equity plan strategies and marine transfer stations

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Okay, going back to our questions.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: So the mayor's racial equity plan highlights two strategies to address waste transfer infrastructure inequities.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: born by overburdened communities.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: The first strategy would be to distribute waste transfer operations such that underutilized stations become more utilized.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: The second would leverage solid waste management contracts as opportunities to produce more distribution of waste transfer contracts.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: How does the department plan to implement these strategies and where can the council help?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Yeah, so I think in part one of the things that we have long been talking about in these hearings is the use of our marine transfer stations for commercial waste.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: That's my next question.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Which as we, I think, discussed maybe in July, we are fully committed to that so long as we can overcome the real financial obstacles there

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: and are planning to do so following the complete implementation of commercial waste zones at the end of next calendar year, which when we first started having these conversations seemed very far away but is now.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: 15 months, which is not that far.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So I think that's the most important thing we can do there is by using excess capacity at specifically the 91st and Southwest Brooklyn Marine Transfer Stations.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: As far as using our procurements to

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: to reduce the capacity in overburdened districts.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: I think that's something that as our current set of waste export contracts starts to expire,

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Because these were all 20-year contracts, we certainly will look at as one of many goals that we want to try to achieve.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: The challenge, again, there are not large waste transfer stations in other neighborhoods, and building a new waste transfer station in New York City

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: is not possible at this moment because of various zoning regulations and permitting requirements.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And so, you know, just to be frank, unless we were to try to build a new municipal waste transfer station and go through the ULERT process for siting and land acquisition,

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: I don't see a new large transfer station that services Department of Sanitation waste opening at any time soon.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks whether Rikers Island could host a new municipal marine transfer station. Anderson says Rikers has only one road in and out, making it better suited as a receiving facility for organic waste by water rather than a truck-based transfer station.
chapters.title: Sanchez asks about Rikers Island as potential transfer or compost site

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Have there been any conversations about trying to open this new municipal marine transfer station at all?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: There have not at this time.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: I think, you know, the thing that we should be looking at as far as new infrastructure is additional composting infrastructure, as we've mentioned before.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And, you know, Rikers Island.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: I was just going to ask, has Rikers Island been spoken about or thought about as a potential place for a new municipal marine transfer station?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: The challenge with Rikers Island as far as being a transfer station is that there's only one road in and one road out.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And so you put a lot of trucks on that one road going to and from the island.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: I think the better option for Rikers Island is to be a receiving facility for...

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: organic waste that's collected and transferred at marine transfer stations all across the city so that it can receive the material by water, not have the additional truck traffic, and then process it into compost that can then be used beneficially.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Is there a way that everything could happen via water if it was at Rikers Island?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Many things can happen via water.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: The thing that can't happen via water is us picking up the trash at 8.5 million residents'homes.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And once the trash is in the truck, it has to go somewhere and dump.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So that's the utility of the transfer station is to then move that material by other means to its processing and disposal location.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So the challenge we always have is...

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: We pick up the trash in the trucks, and somehow the trash has to get out of those trucks.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And so where we do that and how, I think, is the focus of our efforts.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: I think this is a worthy conversation that we should be continuing to explore.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks for updates on increasing barge transport and whether private operators could use marine transfer stations. Anderson says DSNY is looking seriously at this after commercial waste zones are fully implemented and has started conversations about accepting commercial paper at the 59th Street MTS.
chapters.title: Sanchez asks about marine transfer station usage and private operators

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Having said that, are there any updates on increasing usage of marine transfer stations to move additional solid waste via barges in order to shift away from truck-based transport?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Is there any applicability of this program to private operators?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And has there been any discussion of this being scaled up for municipal waste transfer stations?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Again, yes, looking very seriously at doing this after the full implementation.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: of commercial waste zones next year.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: We've already started conversations with our 59th Street MTS, which we don't often talk about, which handles

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: all of our paper that we collect in Manhattan, to see if there would be feasibility for accepting commercial paper, commercial office paper specifically, at that transfer station.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: At this moment, we only have one zone, or I guess now two zones fully rolled out in Manhattan.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So we still need more data on how much commercial office paper is being collected separate from single stream recycling collections.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And as we have that data, we can start to formulate what that would look like.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Have we also had a discussion about collecting all of the paper from the universities that we have on the Isle of Manhattan?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So we haven't looked at universities specifically.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Many of them use private carters, so they would be covered by commercial waste zones.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: The challenge with the 59th Street MTS is that it only takes paper.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Many of the private carters are offering single stream collection where it's paper commingled with metal, glass, and plastic containers.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And so once that's commingled, we can no longer take it at 59th Street because that goes straight to the paper mill on Staten Island.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So we can certainly look into those universities and where their material is going.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: So is there a discussion in which we no longer allow universities to commingle their trash in order to get better streams of flow, trash flow?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: We can certainly have conversations with the universities about how much material they're generating and what kinds of recycling products.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: We will be definitely having that conversation.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks whether DSNY has considered requiring waste transfer stations in designated districts to be enclosed. Anderson says putrescible stations must already be enclosed, non-putrescible stations are not, and DSNY monitors compliance through quarterly reports and inspections.
chapters.title: Sanchez asks about enclosed transfer stations and compliance monitoring

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Has the department considered requiring that waste transfer stations located within the four designated CDs be enclosed?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: That's certainly something we've talked about before.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: All putrescible transfer stations are required to be enclosed today.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: That's a requirement under the state regulatory scheme.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Non-putrescible transfer stations are not required to be enclosed.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: I think as we, and we've talked, I think, a bit before about...

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Taking a more comprehensive look at the construction and demolition industry generally and ways to improve recycling, ways to improve deconstruction rather than demolition.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: I think looking at those facilities and impact that they have on the surrounding community is a great thing to add to that.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: That examination.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Does the department monitor compliance with waste equity law via the quarterly private waste station reports that DSNY receives pursuant to local law 40 of 1990?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Yes, we do.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And then in 2024, the department released a chart detailing the percentage of existing lawfully operating transfer stations in New York City by CD.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Today, what is the breakdown citywide?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Do we have that?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: I don't have that specific report in front of me.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: We release that report every year.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks whether DSNY receives 311 complaints about dust, pests, odors, runoff, open doors, and litter at transfer stations. Anderson says DSNY investigates promptly, usually within eight hours, and conducts weekly and drive-by inspections.
chapters.title: Sanchez asks about 311 complaints and inspections at transfer stations

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And finally, 311.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Please use it.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Does DSNY receive 301 complaints regarding dust, pests, odors, and water or sewer runoff at private solid waste transfer stations?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: What about for things like open doors or gates or for litter adjacent to waste transfer station properties?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Yes, we do receive 301 complaints for all of those categories, and we investigate them quite promptly, usually on the same shift, so within eight hours.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: We also conduct, for most transfer stations, weekly inspections and even more frequent drive-by inspections.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So we'll drive by and look to see are they tracking material out of the facility?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Are the doors open unnecessarily?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Are there odors or other fumes coming out?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And if any of those things are identified, we will take appropriate action.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks for data comparing 311 volumes in environmental justice communities versus non-EJ communities. Anderson says DSNY receives 311 requests from every district but does not have that specific breakdown on hand and can perform the analysis.
chapters.title: Sanchez requests 311 volume data for EJ vs non-EJ communities

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Do you also have, and this is a large data set, but could you help explain if you have the data, the sanitation 311 volumes

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: in environmental, in EJ communities versus non-EJ communities and what that looks like?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Are we making 311 complaints relative to everyone else?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So, yes, everyone makes 311 complaints, every neighborhood in New York City, to the Department of Sanitation, because we have an incredibly high volume of 311, both complaints and service requests.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: It's not all just a complaint.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Sometimes people are asking for something.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So we do see 311 call volume from...

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: every sanitation district and section.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: I don't have specifically in front of me the breakdown between EJ communities and non-EJ communities or between the racial equity communities that are identified in the racial equity

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: report and non-racial equity communities, but we can certainly do that analysis.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: I would really appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: That would be really great.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: I also want to mention, if I have not mentioned, we've been joined by the incomparable Councilmember Chanel Thomas-Henry.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: With her presence, I also want to give a huge plug and shout out.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Roosevelt Avenue needs more trash cans immediately.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: But do you have any questions before?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks what outreach DSNY has done on proper disposal of rechargeable batteries for micromobility devices. Anderson says DSNY works with FDNY and the mayor's office on fire safety education and is awaiting DEC approval of the battery producer responsibility plan.
chapters.title: Sanchez questions battery disposal outreach and education

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: So I want to touch on Councilmember Nurse's rechargeable battery disposal plan.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: What outreach and education has the department engaged in to inform the public of a proper way to dispose of rechargeable batteries for micromobility devices?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Yeah, so we do quite a bit of education.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: This month in particular is Fire Safety Month, and one of the areas of focus this Fire Safety Month is around rechargeable batteries.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So everything from buying UL-approved batteries and making sure that you only have batteries that are safe to use, how to safely store and charge them in your home or business, and how to safely

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: dispose of and recycle them at the end of life.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: The FDNY is doing a lot of education around that this month.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: We are working with them on that education.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: The mayor's office has put out some social media on that.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So those are the kinds of things that we do.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: When the plan from the battery network, which is the producer responsibility organization, is approved by DEC, there are also education components of that that will be

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: undertaken by the producer responsibility organization.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: At this point, DEC has not yet approved that plan.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: We're having ongoing conversations about the right balance between convenience and safety, because obviously we don't want to create drop-off opportunities that then create fire risk and are unsafe for either commercial establishments or for our communities.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So that's an ongoing conversation, but as soon as that plan is approved, we expect that there will be funding there for education as well.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks whether many rechargeable batteries are dropped off at safe disposal events. Anderson says attendance is high and capacity is the challenge, with only one event per borough per year funded; Jen McDonald adds that special waste sites now accept batteries five days a week.
chapters.title: Sanchez asks about safe disposal events and capacity

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And have you, has the department seen a lot of rechargeable batteries dropped off at the safe disposal events?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And if not, what could the department be doing to increase the traffic at safe disposal events?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So I would say the traffic at safe disposal events is never our problem.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: I think our capacity to be able to handle the amount of people that show up is our problem.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Biggest challenge.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And we had a safe disposal event a couple weeks ago during the nor'easter.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And, you know, even though we did advise folks, you know, if it's not safe, don't come out, whatever, we still had over 800 people come.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: to the safe disposal event to try to dispose of paint, batteries, electronics, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So, you know, we would love to increase our capacity for those events.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Right now we're only funded for one per borough per year.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And, you know, we get a lot of volume as far as rechargeable batteries.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Jen, do you have anything to add there?

utterances.speaker: Jen McDonald
utterances.text: I would say that.

utterances.speaker: Jen McDonald
utterances.text: We have seen a great increase in the amount of batteries returned both at the safe events that the commissioner mentioned, but also at the special waste sites that the commissioner mentioned earlier that are now open five days per week.

utterances.speaker: Jen McDonald
utterances.text: That is very convenient for folks to come and bring their batteries in addition to the safe events, which are only one time a year.

utterances.speaker: Jen McDonald
utterances.text: The other point we would make about safety is those drop-off locations are for batteries that are not damaged.

utterances.speaker: Jen McDonald
utterances.text: It is important that damaged batteries, you do contact FDNY to come and...

utterances.speaker: Jen McDonald
utterances.text: Address them because there's a high risk of fire if the battery is damaged, leaking, swelling, obvious heat.

utterances.speaker: Jen McDonald
utterances.text: But as long as the battery, if it's not charging anymore or something like that, it's fine to bring to a safe event or to one of the special waste sites, one in each borough.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks whether DSNY has partnered with other agencies or organizations to host battery disposal events for delivery workers. Anderson says DSNY participates in a micromobility working group with DOT, DCWP, FDNY, and NYPD that addresses safe disposal.
chapters.title: Sanchez asks about partnerships for micromobility battery disposal

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And speaking of FTNY, we're curious, outside of FTNY, has GSNY partnered with any other agency or organization to host events for like deliveristas, for example, looking to safely dispose of their micromobility batteries?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Yeah, so sanitation is part of a micromobility working group that includes many agencies, including the Department of Transportation, Department of Consumer and Worker Protection, FDNY, NYPD,

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: focused on a range of issues around micromobility devices and third-party delivery.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So, yes, that conversation is certainly a part of that work.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And I know when DOT and DCWP are doing some of their outreach to the delivery stick community and to the third-party delivery apps that they're raising the safety and safe disposal issues there as well.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks about the most common waste collection method for public buildings and what share receive off-street collection. Anderson says most city buildings use standard curbside collection, schools use dual-bin trucks, and off-street collection is a relatively low share.
chapters.title: Sanchez asks about city-owned building waste collection methods

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And then we'll talk about intros 30 and 987 quickly before I end with my last question.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: What is the most common method of waste collection for public buildings?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Approximately what percentage of city-owned buildings receive off-street collection and what percentage of school buildings receive off-street collection?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: The most common means of collection is standard curbside collection with a rear-loading collection truck.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Almost every school in New York City, for example, receives a school truck collection.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Those collections are done using dual-bin trucks.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So we pick up a combination of paper recycling, metal, glass, plastic recycling, and organics on various different days.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And then the trash is collected on the neighborhood collection frequency, the same as the surrounding residences.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: As far as the percentage of city buildings that have off-street collection, I don't have that number specifically in front of me, but it's a relatively low share as a percentage of the whole.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks how much it would cost to transition all city-owned buildings to stationary on-street containerization. Anderson says DSNY is working on an estimate but a building-by-building waste generation study would take years; city buildings already use tilt trucks or NYC bins.
chapters.title: Sanchez questions cost and timeline for city building containerization

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Do you have any idea how much it would cost to transition all of the city-owned buildings to stationary on-street containerization?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: I think we're trying to work on that estimate as part of the discussions around this bill.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Two things I'll say.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: One, we do have to do a waste generation study on a building-by-building basis to determine how many bins each building would need.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And so that's a time-consuming process that, you know, if we were to do it, would take, you know, for the whole city, would take several years.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: The second thing is...

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: But just is there any other methodologies that we could use in order to speed track that timeline?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Yeah, we're using a bunch of different approaches.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: We do desktop modeling based on, you know, you can make estimates based on the number of seats in a school, for example, or the number of units in a residential building or the number of meals served.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So we can start from that, but we do have to do the actual detailed waste generation study to make sure that we're putting enough bins there.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Because the last thing we want is to have one bin and then there's a pile of trash sitting next to it because that makes the bin look like it doesn't work.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So we could certainly do that, and we're trying to come up with a reasonable estimate of what the number would be.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: of bins would be and therefore the cost for all city buildings.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: The other thing I'll say, which I mentioned in my testimony, city buildings are already required to containerize their trash.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Every school sets their trash out in tilt trucks if they don't have some other means of containerization already.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Other city buildings are using NYC bins.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: We have a separate contract where city agencies can order NYC bins directly from the vendor, and many city agencies have.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Parks has designed custom waste enclosures that they're using at every park so that there's no longer just piles of bags sort of sitting out by the fence.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So every agency is sort of taking their own approach based on what works for them.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And because we're talking about schools, does that also apply to any of the charter schools as well, or is that solely only for our DOE schools?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: It depends on what kind of charter school and what kind of building they're in.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: If they're in a private building, then they receive commercial waste collection, so they're covered by commercial waste zones.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: If they're in a DOE building, they receive sanitation collection.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: If they're in their own building, many of them do receive sanitation collection, but some of them choose to go with a private charter, so it varies pretty widely based on the specifics of the school.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Great, thank you.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks whether Intro 30's stationary containerization requirements would have effects similar to the M9 pilot. Anderson says containerizing more waste would improve cleanliness and reduce rats, but DSNY is focused on using available trucks for large residential buildings first.
chapters.title: Sanchez asks about containerization effects and Intro 30

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And then, so reports from the M9 containerization pilot indicated record-breaking reductions in rat sightings and improved cleanliness at set-out locations.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Do you believe that the stationary containerization requirements in Intro 30

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: have the similar effect?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: I think anything we can do to containerize more waste would have positive effects as far as cleanliness and rats.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: The thing that we are focused on as we roll out our containerization program citywide by the end of 2031 is where are there still bags sitting on the sidewalk, and that's large residential buildings.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So the approach that we're taking is to, because there's a limited number of trucks that we can purchase any given year, just because the factory that makes these trucks can only make so many.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Our plan right now takes all of those trucks and puts them at solving the residential containerization challenge.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And when we get to the end of 2031 and have purchased all the trucks we need for residential containerization, I think that's the right time to look around.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: say what are other things that we could use Empire bins for, start to look at lower density buildings that maybe could use more shared containers, potentially require shared containers for some of those lower density buildings.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: But anything we do today that takes away from our ability to roll out as quickly as possible on the large residential buildings means we achieve that goal.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks what factors DSNY would consider for association requests for stationary on-street containers. Anderson says DSNY needs enough material to justify the container size and aims for at least 10 to 15 units sharing an Empire bin.
chapters.title: Sanchez asks about factors for Intro 987 association requests

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And then my last question on Majority Leader Bray's Intro 987.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Are there any other factors beyond the department's fleet and collection routes that the department would need to take into consideration when assessing the viability of an association's request for stationary on-street containers?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: I think the other important factor is just is there enough material there to justify the size of the container.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: These containers generally are quite large, and if you had only a handful of single-family homes or a handful of units using one Empire bin, that would probably be a

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: waste of public space for that bin and a waste of cities'money in terms of purchasing the bin and maintaining it.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So we do want to try to get to at least a minimum number of 10 to 15 units sharing the same Empire bin to sort of hit the minimum threshold.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And then from there, we look at waste generation and other factors to determine the right number of bins to assign.

chapters.summary: Sanchez says trucks displaced from the M9 station are parking on side streets and taking resident parking while the M9 lot sits empty. Anderson says he is not familiar with the specific lot but that DSNY has adjusted parking near the M9 garage due to new school pedestrian traffic.
chapters.title: Sanchez raises M9 truck parking and school pedestrian safety

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And speaking of M9, one of my favorite topics, and

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Waste equity.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: My last question is there has been movement of the trucks from M9 because of the new opening of Success Academy Charter School.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And now the trucks that were in front of the M9 station are now just randomly on side streets, taking away all of the local residents parking and just.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Filling our streets with literally blocks of trucks, while the M9 truck storage facility underneath the bridges just sits empty as of right now.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And so curious, has there been more discussion as to be able to move the trucks that are just sitting on the streets back to the empty parking lot that gets only used for things like, you know,

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Harlem Pride.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: I think that there is a greater need for the trucks to be there.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: I mean, you can probably move them for events like Harlem Pride.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: I'm not saying to cancel Harlem Pride.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: But has there been any discussion of being able to move the trucks that are just sitting on the streets back to the M9 parking lot?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with the exact parking lot that you're referring to, but happy to take a look at it.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: We have made some adjustments to the parking around the M9 garage, which, as you have mentioned before, the Manhattan 9 garage is in the Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Bronx 7 and 8 garages are in Manhattan.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: It's sort of a weird dynamic there.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: But they have enclosed spaces.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: It's a much larger facility.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: I think if you were to go up to 215th Street, you would see.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: sanitation trucks parked all over the place.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: But I will say we have tried to rearrange the way that we are parking trucks in the vicinity of the Manhattan Community Board 9 garage because of the additional pedestrian traffic going to and from the new school that opened.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: It's certainly something that we are having active conversations with.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Many council members about because there's a few different districts that sort of cover that area.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And, you know, we want to balance the residents'needs with safe pedestrian travel for the school kids, along with our operational needs to be able to provide service to New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And you know how much I would love to make sure that the M9 trucks are back at Community Board 9 in Manhattan.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: So anything that we can do there would be much appreciated.

chapters.summary: Sanchez thanks Commissioner Anderson and DSNY for testifying. He announces a brief five-minute break before the public session.
chapters.title: Sanchez thanks DSNY and calls five-minute break

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And with that, thank you for surviving another day with us at the Committee of Sanitation and Solid Waste Management.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: I really appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: We will be taking a brief five-minute break and then coming back for our public session.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you, everyone.

utterances.text: So I'm Joyce Bialik, chair of the Plastic Task Force for the Manhattan Solid Waste Advisory Board and a member of WIAC for Environmental Justice that has endorsed my testimony.

utterances.text: I support your oversight of waste equity and environmental justice, 2585, as well as oversight in removal of litter baskets, Bill 1041.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joyce Bialik
utterances.text: So Bill 1041.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joyce Bialik
utterances.text: 1041 will require the sanitation department to consult with the council and community boards before removing litter baskets.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joyce Bialik
utterances.text: With fellow members of WE ACT, I studied disparities in the distribution of baskets based on a community's affluence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joyce Bialik
utterances.text: In 2023, with a larger population in East Harlem, 76K, than in the Upper East Side, 60K, East Harlem had 69 baskets to 2.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joyce Bialik
utterances.text: 60 in the Upper East Side.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joyce Bialik
utterances.text: In addition, only 17% of four street corner baskets were found in East Harlem compared to 95% in the Upper East Side.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joyce Bialik
utterances.text: In our Madison Avenue dirty block study, we found 51% dirty blocks in East Harlem, 6% in the Upper East Side.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joyce Bialik
utterances.text: Less baskets, dirtier blocks, of course.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joyce Bialik
utterances.text: These are environmental justice issues that can be eased with Bill 1041, which will require consultation with community boards before baskets are removed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joyce Bialik
utterances.text: Now just briefly about plastics.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joyce Bialik
utterances.text: There are current council bills addressing plastic designed to reduce plastic in our midst.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joyce Bialik
utterances.text: Plastic is an environmental justice issue.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joyce Bialik
utterances.text: Plastic is produced from fossil fuels.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joyce Bialik
utterances.text: Low-income people of color disproportionately reside near sites where there's drilling and refining for oil and gas, where

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joyce Bialik
utterances.text: toxic chemicals are released, sites that are near polluted rivers and groundwater and near landfills and incinerators.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joyce Bialik
utterances.text: So we seek a hearing for the following council plastic bills, 69, 300, 781, 795.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joyce Bialik
utterances.text: They pertain to plastic beverage containers, artificial turf, and water fountains.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joyce Bialik
utterances.text: Although these bills, they're not introduced.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joyce Bialik
utterances.text: through this committee in order to adhere to 2585 regarding oversight of environmental justice.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joyce Bialik
utterances.text: We are asking you to please reach out to your colleagues to hold hearings for them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joyce Bialik
utterances.text: Thank you so much.
