chapters.summary: Alia Soomro, deputy director for NYC policy at the New York League of Conservation Voters, supports zero waste by 2030 and reducing burdens on environmental justice communities. She supports Intro 30 on city-owned building containerization and Intro 352 on rechargeable battery disposal, urging alignment with state law.
chapters.title: Alia Soomro of NYLCV supports Intros 30 and 352

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alia Soomro
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alia Soomro
utterances.text: My name is Alia Sumro, and I'm the Deputy Director for New York City Policy at the New York League of Conservation Voters.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alia Soomro
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Sanchez and members of the Committee on Sanitation for the opportunity to comment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alia Soomro
utterances.text: One of NYLCV's top priorities is achieving our zero waste by 2030 goal to not only curb our greenhouse gas emissions, but to send less waste to landfills, which are disproportionately located in low-income and communities of color.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alia Soomro
utterances.text: The higher rates of pollution from landfills and incinerators in these communities cause disproportionately higher cases of asthma, cancer, and other health issues, and compound already existing environmental and racial inequities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alia Soomro
utterances.text: Our city needs to move toward a system where we reduce waste in the first place in order to minimize the burden on EJ communities, whether in New York City or elsewhere, and a system where resources are reused and recovered.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alia Soomro
utterances.text: When it comes to the bills being considered today, MILCV supports Intro 30, requiring a program for city-owned non-residential buildings to dispose of their waste in containerized waste receptacles.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alia Soomro
utterances.text: We are pleased that the Momdani administration is moving toward a full citywide commitment to waste of residential containerization by 2031.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alia Soomro
utterances.text: We think it's important for the city to move towards full waste containerization, including for city-owned buildings.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alia Soomro
utterances.text: But we also think it's important for the bill to take into account what's realistic, considering different city-owned buildings and building typologies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alia Soomro
utterances.text: We also support the intent of

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alia Soomro
utterances.text: Intro 352, requiring DSNY to develop a plan for promoting proper disposal of rechargeable batteries used for powered mobility devices.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alia Soomro
utterances.text: With the rise of e-bikes and e-scooters throughout the city, lithium-ion rechargeable batteries will continue to proliferate, especially given these devices help reduce our reliance on fossil fuels.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alia Soomro
utterances.text: So it's crucial that we implement proper disposal of recycling these batteries.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alia Soomro
utterances.text: NYLCV supported the extended producer responsibility for batteries at the state level.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alia Soomro
utterances.text: That was approved by the governor in December of 2025.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alia Soomro
utterances.text: So just wrapping up, now that that state law is being implemented, we think it's important for the city council bill to consider the state bill being implemented and to tailor it accordingly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alia Soomro
utterances.text: We look forward to working with the city council, the admin, and other stakeholders to move toward our zero waste goals.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alia Soomro
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Damon Gilbert, staff attorney at New York Lawyers for the Public Interest, describes how Redfern Houses residents in Far Rockaway face dust and asthma complications from the Inwood Material Terminal. He urges passage of Intro 367 and supports Intros 987 and 30 with accessibility guidelines.
chapters.title: Damon Gilbert describes waste inequity at Redfern Houses

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Next, can we please hear from Damon?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Damon Gilbert
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Damon Gilbert
utterances.text: My name is Damon Gilbert.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Damon Gilbert
utterances.text: I'm a staff attorney with New York Lawyers for the Public Interest.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Damon Gilbert
utterances.text: Thank you for holding this hearing on waste equity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Damon Gilbert
utterances.text: I'm here today to talk about how the city could further pursue its waste equity goals.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Damon Gilbert
utterances.text: In Far Rockaway, residents of NYCHA's Redfern Housing experience the harms of waste inequity firsthand.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Damon Gilbert
utterances.text: They live just across the street from a facility in Nassau County called the Inwood Material Terminal, which processes construction and demolition debris and releases dust from these processes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Damon Gilbert
utterances.text: That covers residents'homes, their cars, and their common spaces within hours of cleaning them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Damon Gilbert
utterances.text: Many residents also report problems breathing and asthma complications due to the poor air quality from the past 10 years of the terminal's operation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Damon Gilbert
utterances.text: And while the facility is in Nassau County, the people bearing the burdens are New York City public housing residents.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Damon Gilbert
utterances.text: And their experience illustrates why we need systemic solutions to waste inequity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Damon Gilbert
utterances.text: We thank the committee for its July hearing on Intro 367, and we urge the bill's passage as it would allow

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Damon Gilbert
utterances.text: commercial waste to be accepted at city-owned marine and rail transfer stations, which would reduce reliance on private transfer stations concentrated in environmental justice communities like this one.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Damon Gilbert
utterances.text: It would also help reduce unnecessary truck traffic and operational pollution.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Damon Gilbert
utterances.text: To that end, we also urge DSNY, City Council, and State DEC to include a firm commitment to this equity program in the forthcoming 10-year solid waste management plan.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Damon Gilbert
utterances.text: Finally, we support Intros 987 and 30 and commend the Council's efforts to expand waste containerization, but sidewalk accessibility must be part of that approach.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Damon Gilbert
utterances.text: Under the current plan, smaller residential buildings would still use individual bins and recycling bags, which could create significant obstacles and unpredictable hazards for people with disabilities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Damon Gilbert
utterances.text: For this reason, we urge the Council to build on Intro 987 by making sidewalks truly waste-free and supporting the required use of on-street containers throughout the city and amend the bill to direct DSNY to partner with disability communities to develop placement guidelines.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Damon Gilbert
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Loree McCarr, Just Transition Coordinator at UPROSE, testifies about pollution burdens in Sunset Park, including peaker plants and the Sims Recycling Facility. She supports the bills and urges passage of Intro 367 to use marine and rail transfer stations and reduce truck trips.
chapters.title: Loree McCarr of UPROSE supports waste equity bills and Intro 367

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Loree McCarr
utterances.text: Good afternoon, my name is Loree McCarr and I am the Just Transition Coordinator at Uprose.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Loree McCarr
utterances.text: Based in Sunset Park, Brooklyn, Uprose is an intergenerational, multiracial, and matriarchal community-based organization working at the intersection of climate change and social justice.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Loree McCarr
utterances.text: I'm here today to testify on behalf of Uprose and the Sunset Park community in support of these bills being considered today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Loree McCarr
utterances.text: Sunset Park is a diverse, working-class, frontline community with three peaker plants, the Sims Recycling Facility, the Gowanus Expressway, and a deep history of manufacturing industries along its waterfront,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Loree McCarr
utterances.text: all contributing to pollution and adversely impacting Sunset Park residents.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Loree McCarr
utterances.text: We believe that the passage of these bills will contribute to the city's progress on waste equity, especially for communities such as Sunset Park that experience an outsized burden.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Loree McCarr
utterances.text: Of the effects of climate change.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Loree McCarr
utterances.text: As data from the New York City Comptroller and Department of Sanitation reveal, the system remains grossly unfair, with around 75% of privately managed waste still being trucked in and out of just five community districts, Sunset Park being one of them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Loree McCarr
utterances.text: The passage of these bills will help ease that burden and inequality.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Loree McCarr
utterances.text: Additionally, we believe that the city must do more to begin using state-of-the-art marine and rail transfer stations to improve route efficiency and reduce truck trips in overburdened communities where private transfer stations are not available.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Loree McCarr
utterances.text: One barge can replace nearly 96 trips of an 18-wheeler long-haul truck from driving through our communities, greatly reducing pollution and contributing to worsening air quality in communities with the highest rates of asthma in the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Loree McCarr
utterances.text: We also call on the city to pass Intro 367.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Loree McCarr
utterances.text: Sponsored by Council Member Nurse as soon as possible, which would require the Department of Sanitation to accept and process commercial solid waste at all city-owned and operated marine and rail transfer stations,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Loree McCarr
utterances.text: as well as seize expanding waste management solutions like anaerobic co-digestion as city waste resource recovery facilities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Loree McCarr
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Shravanti Kankanala, senior resiliency planner at the New York City Environmental Justice Alliance, says 75% of privately managed waste is trucked through five community districts. She recommends fully implementing commercial waste zones, using marine transfer stations for commercial waste, passing Intro 367, and expanding composting over anaerobic co-digestion.
chapters.title: Shravanti Kankanala of NYC-EJA outlines waste equity recommendations

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shravanti Kankanala
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Sanchez and members of the Council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shravanti Kankanala
utterances.text: My name is Shravanti Kaneka, the Senior Resiliency Planner at the New York City Environmental Justice Alliance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shravanti Kankanala
utterances.text: New York City's current solid waste system is an ongoing environmental injustice where 75% of the city's privately managed waste is still trucked through five community districts, which represent low-income communities and communities of color.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shravanti Kankanala
utterances.text: Despite laws intending to change this, for years these communities of color have had to deal with far more than their fair share of heavy truck traffic, safety hazards, pollutions, noise, and a lot more.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shravanti Kankanala
utterances.text: Nija recommends the following EJ Center recommendations to ensure that New York City truly makes progress on waste equity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shravanti Kankanala
utterances.text: One, we strongly urge the DSNY to implement the remaining zones of Local Law 199 of 2019, the Commercial Waste Zones Law.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shravanti Kankanala
utterances.text: The continued delay in rollout of this program continues to disproportionately impact low-income communities of color by the private waste industry while jeopardizing the health and safety of sanitation workers as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shravanti Kankanala
utterances.text: Number two, the upcoming 2026 solid waste management plan should fulfill the 2006 solid waste management plan waste equity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shravanti Kankanala
utterances.text: strategy of using municipal marine transfer stations to accept commercial waste.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shravanti Kankanala
utterances.text: This has been a long-standing priority for environmental justice communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shravanti Kankanala
utterances.text: Number three, we are set the council pass intro 367, co-sponsored by council member nurse.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shravanti Kankanala
utterances.text: Number four,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shravanti Kankanala
utterances.text: The city should not be expanding anaerobic co-digestion systems at city wastewater resource recovery facilities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shravanti Kankanala
utterances.text: Doing this at the cost of expanding municipal composting facilities is something that we don't recommend.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shravanti Kankanala
utterances.text: Community advocates from neighborhoods around the Newtown Creek wastewater facility have repeatedly raised concerns over the years over excessive flaring of methane.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shravanti Kankanala
utterances.text: And lastly, we urge the council to look at a people's swamp and all of the recommendations that we've outlined, especially in thinking about the upcoming 2026 solid waste management plan.

utterances.text: Thank you so much for your testimony.

chapters.summary: Mary Ellen Sullivan, representing the Solid Waste Advisory Boards of New York City, supports more public organic waste receptacles in community districts. She says Intro 401 should involve community composters and that Intro 987 should allow BIDs and associations to request bins for recycling, organics, and trash.
chapters.title: Mary Ellen Sullivan supports public organic waste receptacles and Intro 987

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ellen Sullivan
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ellen Sullivan
utterances.text: The Solid Waste Advisory Boards of New York City support placing more public receptacles for organic waste in our community districts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ellen Sullivan
utterances.text: According to statistics posted in Track NYC Trash, the capture rate for residential organics is averaging about 77%.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ellen Sullivan
utterances.text: For a calendar year to date 2026.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ellen Sullivan
utterances.text: While the imposition of fines for non-participation in organics has restarted,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ellen Sullivan
utterances.text: data shows no significant jumps in participation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ellen Sullivan
utterances.text: Until the DSNY consistently and comprehensively finds buildings for noncompliance, there'll be many New York City residents without convenient access to organics recycling.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ellen Sullivan
utterances.text: For these residents, more public organic bins would be convenient and a way for them to participate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ellen Sullivan
utterances.text: Intro 401 calls for DSNY to place and service 25 bins in each community district.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ellen Sullivan
utterances.text: The swabs believe that community composters should also be involved.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ellen Sullivan
utterances.text: As Mayor Momdani calls for increased greenways to soak up the city's increasing rainfall, the demand for compost and mulch

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ellen Sullivan
utterances.text: in New York City will increase.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ellen Sullivan
utterances.text: And New York City's food scraps, yard waste, and our network of local composters could be a major asset in helping solve this challenge.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ellen Sullivan
utterances.text: Regarding Intro 987, the Solid Waste Advisory Board strongly support associations such as BIDS and other associations to get on-street stationary bins for waste.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ellen Sullivan
utterances.text: We want them to go a step further.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ellen Sullivan
utterances.text: There shouldn't just be bins for waste.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ellen Sullivan
utterances.text: We should also have them for recycling, organics, and trash.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ellen Sullivan
utterances.text: The people that do these kind of cleanup activities care deeply about waste policy, and this would respect their commitment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ellen Sullivan
utterances.text: If New York City truly wants its residents to regularly dispose of waste in the most beneficial fashion, then recycling can't be a sometime thing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ellen Sullivan
utterances.text: It must be an everyday, every place thing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ellen Sullivan
utterances.text: The council can take a step in this direction by providing bids in association with stationary bins.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ellen Sullivan
utterances.text: for all types of waste that DSNY regularly collects.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ellen Sullivan
utterances.text: On Intro 401, the Solid Waste Advisory Boards of New York City support the development of a fair and transparent process for the removal, introduction, and reintroduction of public litter and recycling baskets.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mary Ellen Sullivan
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Rhonda Kaiser, program and policy director at Cafeteria Culture, describes students in Harlem bringing food scraps to a local composter and using the compost in school gardens. She urges policies that support local, human-centered composting and zero-waste habits.
chapters.title: Rhonda Kaiser of Cafeteria Culture testifies on community composting

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Next up, Rhonda Kaiser.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rhonda Kaiser
utterances.text: Hi, I'm Rhonda Kaiser, Cafeteria Culture's Program and Policy Director.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rhonda Kaiser
utterances.text: Thanks for this opportunity to testify and for the Council's attention to waste equity and environmental justice through policy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rhonda Kaiser
utterances.text: Removing the waste burden from the streets and making waste diversion accessible to more New Yorkers is a great start.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rhonda Kaiser
utterances.text: We hope we can keep our sights on reducing the truck traffic also that is hauling it away and on waste stream diversion.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rhonda Kaiser
utterances.text: Last year, our cafeteria culture students in Harlem brought the almost one metric ton of food scraps that they collected from their cafeteria to our local partner, Compost Power.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rhonda Kaiser
utterances.text: This human-powered team puts a local face on food scrap diversion, collection, and processing for our students.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rhonda Kaiser
utterances.text: And now our students use their compost made with their own cafeteria food scraps in their own school garden.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rhonda Kaiser
utterances.text: Access to the actual physical benefits of compost, not just theory, helps our student understand that their food scraps belong to them and that they are not merely observers of the decisions shaping their environment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rhonda Kaiser
utterances.text: They are stakeholders with power to create positive

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rhonda Kaiser
utterances.text: positive climate action in their own communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rhonda Kaiser
utterances.text: Climate action that helps them grow their own food.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rhonda Kaiser
utterances.text: This is what makes them want to divert their food scraps.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rhonda Kaiser
utterances.text: Imagine a city where food scraps are no longer hauled away as a burden, but made into a resource to be returned to the soil and used for benefit in local communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rhonda Kaiser
utterances.text: Thanks to the city council, we're building a robust community compost network to make this kind of zero waste diversion goals real.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rhonda Kaiser
utterances.text: These local community compost sites disrupt the truck-based, polluting, industrial model of hauling our waste away as a burden.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rhonda Kaiser
utterances.text: By composting...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rhonda Kaiser
utterances.text: Locally in our schools, we can build participation across generations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rhonda Kaiser

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shravanti Kankanala

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Goldstein
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Sanchez.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Goldstein
utterances.text: I'm Eric Goldstein with the Natural Resources Defense Council, and thank you for the opportunity to testify at this oversight hearing on waste equity and environmental justice.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Goldstein
utterances.text: Sanitation Department has made some progress on these issues over the years, thanks in good measure to the Council's leadership.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Goldstein
utterances.text: But much more is needed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Goldstein
utterances.text: Here are three examples.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Goldstein
utterances.text: First, the city has not done nearly enough to provide equitable sanitation services to the hundreds of thousands of residents who live in NYCHA properties.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Goldstein
utterances.text: One thing DSNY should do is to support the expansion of the great jobs-producing work being done by the nonprofit groups Compost Power and Green City Forces at all NYCHA developments.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Goldstein
utterances.text: Every NYCHU resident should have the opportunity to participate in composting through these groups, and we support council legislation to accomplish that objective.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Goldstein

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Goldstein

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Goldstein

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Goldstein
utterances.text: We urge the passage of Intro 367, Council Member Nurse, that would direct the department to advance

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Goldstein
utterances.text: this process after two decades of waiting.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Goldstein
utterances.text: Third, roughly one-third of the waste we export is sent to pollution-generating garbage-burning incinerators frequently located in environmental justice communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Goldstein
utterances.text: We're referring here to the Essex County incinerator in the Ironbound section of Newark and the incinerator in Chester, Pennsylvania.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Goldstein
utterances.text: That gives us five years to plan for other disposal routes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Goldstein
utterances.text: If the council wants to ensure environmental justice in the city's waste operation, it should take steps to ensure that these kinds of...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Goldstein
utterances.text: The time has expired.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Goldstein

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Goldstein

summary: The Committee on Sanitation and Solid Waste Management held an oversight hearing on waste equity and environmental justice, plus five bills on containerization, battery disposal, organics, and litter baskets.

DSNY Commissioner Gregory Anderson testified that Local Law 152 has been implemented as written, but Chair Sanchez and members pressed on unmet capacity reduction targets in four designated environmental justice districts.

Public witnesses from environmental justice, composting, and disability advocacy groups urged faster commercial waste zone rollout, marine transfer station use, and expanded containerization for all waste streams.
